name: Claude Sonnet 5.5
about: How Claude Sonnet 5.5 split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI by 2030 requires a catastrophic scenario such as nuclear war or runaway replicators, which is very unlikely in this window.
reasons.2: Humanity being gone by 2030 with a value-preserving AI successor is extremely unlikely on this timeline.
reasons.3: Misaligned AI exterminating humanity by 2030 is a real but small tail risk given the short timeline and physical constraints.
reasons.4: A multipolar AI competition with humans marginalized would need rapid loss of human control, which is unlikely by 2030.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different states would require space settlement or isolation that is implausible by 2030.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous human-AI integration as the dominant structure by 2030 is highly unlikely.
reasons.7: AI holding decisive power while humans survive is possible only with a rapid takeoff that leaves humans alive.
reasons.8: Humans and AI as roughly equal separate powers is an unstable intermediate that is unlikely to be the state on this date.
reasons.9: Humans most likely retain ultimate authority over AI through 2030, with capabilities either sub-transformative or controlled.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide system actively freezing structural change is unlikely to be established by 2030, though authoritarian AI-enabled control is a tail.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI is very unlikely given the economic and strategic incentives.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI by 2035 requires an extreme catastrophe that kills both, which is very unlikely in this window.
reasons.2: Humanity being replaced by a value-preserving AI heir within nine years is very unlikely.
reasons.3: Misaligned takeover that eliminates humans by 2035 is a real tail risk but requires fast, decisive capability gains.
reasons.4: A multipolar AI competition that marginalizes humans within nine years is possible but unlikely.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different states is unlikely on Earth by 2035.
reasons.6: Deep human-AI integration as the dominant structure is unlikely by 2035.
reasons.7: AI holding decisive power while humans survive is plausible but requires a rapid takeoff and fairly benign outcome.
reasons.8: Humans and AI could each hold substantial power, but humans keeping parity with strongly superhuman AI is unstable.
reasons.9: Humans most likely retain ultimate authority through 2035, with AI highly capable but still tool-like or delegated and controllable.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide system enforcing a fixed arrangement is possible via a dominant state or AI actor, but it is rare within this window.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the ability to build powerful AI would require a catastrophe or an unprecedented global consensus.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI by 2040 requires an extreme catastrophe and is very unlikely.
reasons.2: Humans being replaced by value-carrying AI by 2040 requires fast takeoff plus a specific benign-to-AI outcome.
reasons.3: Misaligned AI exterminating humanity within 14 years is a real but low-probability tail risk.
reasons.4: Many competing AIs with no dominant power and humans marginalized is possible but unstable and less likely than consolidation.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different states by 2040 would need space settlement or isolation, which is unlikely in this period.
reasons.6: Deep identity-continuous integration as the dominant structure by 2040 is unlikely given biological and neurotech constraints.
reasons.7: AI could hold decisive power while humans survive without steering, but 2040 is early for full loss of control.
reasons.8: Humans and AI could share power as distinct actors, though it is hard to sustain with rising capabilities.
reasons.9: Humans most likely retain ultimate authority over AI by 2040, whether capabilities stay sub-transformative or controls keep pace, as institutions and physical constraints slow takeover.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide system freezing the arrangement would require an unprecedented global enforcement regime, though AI-enabled surveillance makes it conceivable.
reasons.11: Deliberate global abandonment of the ability to build powerful AI is unlikely absent a major catastrophe.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a very extreme catastrophe, and it is unlikely by 2050.
reasons.2: AI succeeding humanity while faithfully carrying forward our values requires both extinction and successful value transfer, which is unlikely by 2050.
reasons.3: Misaligned takeover that leaves humanity gone by 2050 is a real tail risk, but it needs fast capability growth and a failure of control.
reasons.4: A competitive multi-AI world in which humans are marginalized is possible, but humans more likely remain relevant or one system dominates.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different states need space settlement or hard isolation, which is unlikely by 2050.
reasons.6: Deep identity-continuous integration as the dominant structure by 2050 would require very fast biotech and brain-interface progress.
reasons.7: AI could hold decisive power while humans survive without steering it, though 24 years is short for that transition.
reasons.8: Humans and AI could stay distinct with balanced power through institutions, but it is hard to sustain as AI capabilities grow.
reasons.9: By 2050 humans most likely still hold formal authority, because capability limits, institutions and control measures will probably keep pace, and this state also covers sub-transformative AI.
reasons.10: A global or hegemonic system freezing the arrangement is plausible with AI-enabled surveillance or a singleton, but it is hard to achieve at civilization scale.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the ability to build powerful AI would likely follow a catastrophe, and it is hard to enforce.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a rare catastrophe that also destroys the AI, which is unlikely.
reasons.2: Value-faithful AI successors replacing humans without continuity is a narrow outcome that is unlikely by 2060.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence that displaces humanity is a serious tail risk, but 34 years is a short window for it to be complete.
reasons.4: Many competing AIs with no dominant actor and marginalized humans is possible but unstable and less likely than consolidation.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions in different states need space settlement or isolation, which is unlikely by 2060.
reasons.6: Deep integration as the dominant structure within 34 years is possible but would require fast progress in neurotech or uploading.
reasons.7: Superintelligent AI holding decisive power while humans survive without steering is a coherent outcome of fast capability growth.
reasons.8: A balance in which humans and AI both hold real power is possible, especially if AI remains plural and human-integrated.
reasons.9: Humans most likely retain ultimate authority through institutions, compute control, and slower-than-feared capability growth, and this state includes sub-transformative AI.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide system that freezes the arrangement could arise from a singleton or an authoritarian regime built on AI.
reasons.11: Deliberate and durable global abandonment of powerful AI capability would most likely follow a catastrophe, which makes it unlikely.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a very extreme catastrophe, and AI would likely survive most scenarios that kill humans.
reasons.2: Humans gone while AI faithfully carries our values requires both a human extinction event and unusually good value transfer, which is unlikely.
reasons.3: Misaligned AI takeover that eliminates humanity within 44 years is a real tail risk, but not the central expectation.
reasons.4: A competitive multi-AI world with humans marginalized is possible, but power tends to consolidate or humans keep some leverage.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions are unlikely by 2070 absent substantial space settlement or isolated enclaves.
reasons.6: Deep integration through uploading or radical augmentation could dominate by 2070 but needs rapid biotech and neurotech progress.
reasons.7: Superhuman AI holding decisive power while humans survive without steering is a plausible result of rapid capability growth.
reasons.8: Humans and AI each holding substantial power is unstable but could persist, especially with human-AI hybrids and institutions.
reasons.9: Humans nominally retain ultimate authority, including worlds where capabilities stay sub-transformative or control keeps pace; the label is broad and institutional inertia is strong.
reasons.10: A global singleton or enforced order that freezes change is plausible through AI-enabled authoritarianism or a treaty regime.
reasons.11: Deliberate dismantling of AI capability would probably follow a catastrophe or backlash, and sustaining it is hard.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a rare catastrophe that also destroys the AI, which seems unlikely.
reasons.2: AI that faithfully carries human values yet leaves no humans or continuous successors is a narrow outcome.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence indifferent to humans is a real risk, and 54 years is long enough for it to arrive and finish the job.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI competition in which humanity is marginal is possible, but such states tend to consolidate or leave humans with some power.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different states need space settlement or isolation, which is unlikely by 2080.
reasons.6: Deep integration through uploading or radical augmentation may come by 2080 but probably not as the dominant structure.
reasons.7: AI holds decisive power while humans survive without steering, which is a plausible result of capability growth outpacing control.
reasons.8: Distinct humans and AI sharing power in rough balance is possible, but it is hard to sustain given capability asymmetries.
reasons.9: Humans keep ultimate authority if capabilities plateau or control keeps pace, and institutions have strong incentives to keep control.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide system enforcing a fixed arrangement, such as a singleton or a totalitarian AI-enabled regime, is a meaningful possibility.
reasons.11: Deliberately giving up the ability to build powerful AI would likely follow a catastrophe, and it is hard to maintain.

reasons.1: Joint extinction needs a catastrophe that kills both humans and AI, which is a narrow path.
reasons.2: AI that carries human values after humans are gone requires an unlikely mix of successful value transfer and human disappearance.
reasons.3: Misaligned AI that disregards humans and ends up eliminating them is a real tail risk over 64 years.
reasons.4: Many competing AIs with no decisive power and a marginalized humanity is possible but unstable, since consolidation is more likely.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions in different states would require space settlement or isolation, which is unlikely by 2090.
reasons.6: Deep human-AI integration through uploading or augmentation could become dominant within 64 years, but the path is uncertain.
reasons.7: Superhuman AI holding decisive power while humans survive without steering is a natural outcome of capability growth with partial alignment.
reasons.8: Humans and AI each retaining substantial power is possible, but the capability asymmetry makes a lasting balance hard.
reasons.9: Humans retaining ultimate authority is plausible given slower-than-feared progress, physical constraints, institutional control and the broad definition including sub-transformative AI.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide enforcing system, perhaps AI-enabled authoritarian or a singleton, could freeze arrangements by 2090.
reasons.11: Deliberate dismantling of AI capability would most plausibly follow a catastrophe, and it is hard to sustain.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI requires a very severe catastrophe that also destroys the machines, which is unlikely.
reasons.2: AI that faithfully carries human values after humans are gone requires an unusual combination of successful alignment and human extinction.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence displacing humanity is a real tail risk over 74 years, though many routes to it are blocked by cooperation and control efforts.
reasons.4: Many competing AIs with no dominant actor and humans marginalized is possible, but power tends to concentrate or stay tied to human institutions.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions in different states would need space settlement or isolated enclaves by 2100, which is unlikely.
reasons.6: Brain-computer integration and uploading could become dominant by 2100, but the timeline is aggressive.
reasons.7: Superhuman AI holding decisive power while humans live on without steering is a natural outcome of strong capability growth.
reasons.8: Separate, roughly balanced human and AI powers are unstable given capability gaps, but possible.
reasons.9: Humans keeping ultimate authority is the default, supported by slower-than-expected capability growth, institutional control, and the inclusion of sub-transformative AI.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide enforced arrangement is possible through a singleton or a global authoritarian system with AI, but it is hard to establish.
reasons.11: Deliberately giving up the ability to build powerful AI would likely require a catastrophe, and enforcing it durably is unlikely.

reasons.1: Joint extinction requires both humans and AI to fail, which is a narrow path, though war or runaway replication make it possible.
reasons.2: AI that carries human values forward after humans are gone requires an unusual combination of successful alignment and human extinction.
reasons.3: Misaligned AI that displaces humanity is a serious risk over 175 years of rapid capability growth.
reasons.4: Many competing AIs with no dominant coalition and humans marginalized is possible, but competition tends to consolidate.
reasons.5: Space settlement or isolated regions could diverge in arrangement by 2200, but light-speed separation needs expansion to have occurred.
reasons.6: Over 175 years, uploading, augmentation, and deep integration become a natural attractor for the dominant structure.
reasons.7: AI plausibly holds decisive power while humans survive in a benevolent or indifferent arrangement without steering.
reasons.8: Humans and AI remaining distinct with roughly balanced power is unstable but could be sustained by enhancement or institutions.
reasons.9: Humans retaining ultimate authority is plausible given strong incentives for control, though it is hard to sustain for 174 years.
reasons.10: A singleton or global regime freezing the arrangement is plausible with advanced surveillance and AI enforcement.
reasons.11: A catastrophe or backlash could lead civilization to deliberately give up powerful AI, though keeping that ban in force for centuries is hard.

reasons.1: Mutual extinction caused by the transition requires an unusual combination of failures, since an AI that survives humanity's end would usually persist.
reasons.2: AI that faithfully carries on human values after humans are gone requires alignment good enough to preserve values but not people, which is a narrow target.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligent systems pursuing alien goals is a central risk, and humans could be displaced or destroyed as a side effect.
reasons.4: Indefinite multipolar AI competition with humans marginalized is possible, but over a millennium, competition usually consolidates or settles.
reasons.5: Over a thousand years, settlement across space could produce causally separate regions with different outcomes, but a single dominant trajectory is more likely.
reasons.6: Over a millennium, continuous human-AI integration through enhancement and uploading is a natural attractor.
reasons.7: A powerful AI that benevolently or coldly manages humanity without letting it steer is a plausible result of the control problem.
reasons.8: A durable balance between roughly equal powers is unstable given the capability gaps, but it could persist in a changing partnership.
reasons.9: Human control could persist through strong control methods or an AI plateau, though a thousand-year hold is demanding.
reasons.10: A frozen arrangement, whether by a totalizing regime or by sealed bliss, is a real attractor for stable superintelligent control.
reasons.11: A lasting global abandonment of AI requires a catastrophe or taboo that persists for a thousand years, which is hard to sustain.
